body_md:
\label{re:2.13}
Suppose that all hypotheses of Proposition \ref{pro:2.12} hold. Suppose further that the coincidence set has nonempty interior. Then all free boundary points are regular
(cf.\ \cite{PSU} for the definition of regular points.) Applying Proposition \ref{pro:2.11}, for any $x_0\in \Gamma(u)$, we see that  the free boundary $\Gamma(u)$ is a
$C^{1,\alpha}$ graph near $x_0$.

label: le:2.2
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{le:2.2}
Let $u\in C(\mathcal{C}_{2}^+)$ satisfy
$$
\left\{\begin{split}
\mathcal{L}u&=0 \quad\mbox{in}\quad \mathcal{C}_{2}^+,\\
u&=0\quad\mbox{on}\quad \{x_n=0\}\cap\partial \mathcal{C}_{2}^+,\\
u&=1\quad\mbox{on}\quad \{x_n=1\}\cap\partial \mathcal{C}_{2}^+,\\
u&>0\quad\mbox{in}\quad \mathcal{C}_{2}^+,
\end{split}\right.
$$
where $\mathcal{C}_{2}^+:=\mathcal{C}_{2,2}(0)\cap\{x_n>0\}$ denotes a cylinder; see Notations (2).

Then
\begin{equation}\label{E3.22}
\partial_n u(0)\geq C,
\end{equation}
where $C>0$ is a constant depending only on $\lambda$, $\Lambda$, and the dimension $n$.

label: le:2.6
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Without loss of generality, we assume in addition that the origin $0\in\Omega^{c}(u)$. For any unit vector $\tau\in V(u)$, Lemma \ref{le:2.4} implies that the ray
$\{\mathbb{R}_+\tau\}\subseteq\Omega^{c}(u).$ Hence $\mathbb{R}_+V(u)$ is a cone.

We verify that the cone is convex. Choosing $x_1,x_2\in\mathbb{R}_+V(u)$, let
$$
x_{\theta}:=\theta x_1+(1-\theta)x_2,\qquad \forall\theta\in (0,1).
$$
We want to show $x_{\theta}\in\mathbb{R}_+V(u)$. Once we verify that $sx_{\theta}\in\Omega^{c}(u)$ for any $s\geq 0$, this result follows. In fact, Lemma \ref{le:2.4} implies that
$sx_{1},sx_{2}\in\Omega^{c}(u)$. Since $u\geq 0$ in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$, $u(sx_{\theta})=0$ follows from the convexity of $u$.

Assume now that we have unit vectors $\{\nu_k\}_{k=1}^{\infty}\subset V(u)$ with $\nu_k\rightarrow\nu$. Then there exists
$\{P^{k}_{j}\}_{j=1}^{\infty}\subset\Omega^{c}(u)$ such that
$$
P^{k}_{j}/|P^{k}_{j}|\rightarrow \nu_k \qquad\mbox{as}\quad j\rightarrow +\infty.
$$
Taking a subsequence if necessary, we have
$$
P^{k}_{j}/|P^{k}_{j}|\rightarrow\nu\qquad \mbox{as}\quad j, k\rightarrow +\infty.
$$
Then we deduce that $\nu\in V(u)$, that is, the cone $\mathbb{R}_+V(u)$ is closed.

label: cor: 4.1
title: Corollary

title: Proof
body_md:
Assuming by contradiction that $\mathrm{Int}\,\Omega^{c}(u)=\emptyset$, we have proved $u(x)=\frac{1}{2}x^TAx$ in the previous section. Then $\mbox{det}(A)=0$ comes from $V(u)\neq\emptyset$, i.e., $u$ is a lower dimensional global solution. This contradicts one of our assumptions.

Next we show that (\ref{E4.8}) holds. On the contrary, we suppose that (\ref{E4.8}) fails. By Proposition \ref{pro:2.12}, we see that $u$ is convex.
Since $\mathbb{R}_+V(u)$ is a closed cone (see Lemma \ref{le:2.6}), we may choose unit vectors $\pm e\in V(u)$. By Lemma \ref{le:2.4}, we have $\pm(\partial_e u)\leq 0$.
Hence $u$ is a lower dimensional function, a contradiction.

title: Proof
body_md:
When $\operatorname{Int}\Omega^{c}(u)=\emptyset$, we have $u(x)=\frac{1}{2}x^TAx$. It remains to consider the case $\operatorname{Int}\Omega^{c}(u)\neq\emptyset$.

 Consider the one dimensional case $n=1$. If $\Omega^{c}(u)$ is compact, its convexity forces $\Omega^{c}(u)$ to be a closed interval. If $\Omega^{c}(u)$ is non-compact, together with $\Gamma(u)\neq\emptyset$ and the convexity of $\Omega^{c}(u)$, we find that $\Omega^{c}(u)$ is a ray in $\mathbb{R}^{1}$.
Upon translating and rotating coordinates, $u$ takes the form (\ref{E1.5}).

Next we consider the case $n\geq 2$. Under the assumption that $\operatorname{MD}(\Omega^{c}(u))<+\infty,$ invoking Theorem \ref{le:4.1}, we deduce that either
$u\in\mathcal{G}_c$, or $u$ is a lower dimensional global solution. If $u\in\mathcal{G}_c$, then $\Omega^{c}(u)$ is a compact convex set. As already mentioned in
Remark \ref{re:2.13}, the local $C^{1,\alpha}$ regularity of the free boundary follows. Using a simple compactness argument, we conclude that $\Omega^c(u)$ is a $C^{1,\alpha}$ domain.

Under the assumption that $\operatorname{MD}(\Omega^{c}(u))=+\infty,$ we have $V(u)\neq\emptyset$. Assuming that $u$ is not a lower dimensional global solution, by a suitable
translation and rotation of the coordinate system, we obtain $V(u)=\{-e_n\}$, where we appeal to Theorem \ref{thm:thm4.1}. Hence $\partial_n u\geq 0$. It is easily seen that $u\in\mathcal{G}_{\infty}$. Otherwise, suppose that $\partial_{\tau}u\geq 0$ for some $\tau\neq e_n$. Using $u(0)=0$, we get $u(-\mathbb{R}_{+}\tau)\equiv 0$, i.e.,
$-\tau\in V(u)$, a contradiction, as we wanted to see.

The inclusion (a) is trivial. We have already shown that inclusion (b) holds; see Lemma \ref{lemma 4.11}. It remains to verify (\ref{E1.18}). In fact, the first limit follows from $\operatorname{MD}(\Omega^{c}(u))=+\infty$. The second limit was established in the proof of Lemma \ref{lemma 4.11}; see (\ref{E4.103}). For $n=2$, the third limit
is trivial. For $n\geq 3$, given sufficiently small $\epsilon>0$, by (\ref{E5.60}) and (\ref{E4.100}), we find that
 \begin{equation*}
 \left\{\begin{split}
\rho_k^{-1}\mbox{diam}(\Omega^{c}_{k}(u))<\mbox{diam}(\Omega^{c}(v))+\epsilon,\\
\rho_k^{-1}\operatorname{MD}(\Omega^{c}_{k}(u))>\operatorname{MD}(\Omega^{c}(v))-\epsilon,
\end{split}\right.
\qquad\mbox{for}\quad k\gg 1.
 \end{equation*}
By Theorem \ref{thm:5}, we have
 \begin{equation*}
\mbox{diam}\big(\Omega^{c}(v)\big)/\operatorname{MD}\big(\Omega^{c}(v)\big)= C(A_{n-1},F).
\end{equation*}
Hence the third limit follows. The proof is complete.
